en: In the *Śaiśirīya* tradition, the great seer Vyāḍi himself will explain the eight types of phonetic modifications, beginning with *jaṭā*, in the work titled *Jaṭāpaṭalakārikā*, without excessive detail.
The matted locks, the garland, the crest, the line, the banner, the staff, the chariot, and the cloud—
these eight distortions have been declared by the wise in their proper sequence. One should speak of this kind of sequence even when there is a reversal of order.
The wise one, having understood the characteristic sequence of the transformation known as the *jaṭā*, should indeed recite the sequence three times, both in direct and reverse order.
In the reverse order, the sandhi should be like that of the words; in the direct order, it should be according to the sequence.

Regarding the change of *ṣ* to *ṣ*, the change to *ṇ*, and lengthening that is prescribed for sequential sandhi, those should not be applied when the order is reversed; rather, there should be vowel-accentuation, *kṣaipra*-svarita, and so forth.
In a reverse sequence, the sandhi is like that of individual words, even when they are not joined in their usual order.
It should be abandoned in regular order and sequence; one should recite it out of order like a word.

In the fourfold sequence, the threefold sequence, and likewise in the fivefold sequence, one should speak of the middle as threefold by means of the beginning and the end through the reversals of the sequence.

Just as [the sequence] exists at the beginning of the *samaya* and likewise after the *samaya*, so too one should transform that which resides in the matted locks (*jaṭā*) at the beginning of the *samaya* by means of the pure [state]. There is no progression of the *samaya* without the sequence beginning with the *samaya*.
One should recite that *trikrama* together with the first [syllable] situated at the beginning of the *samaya* and so forth.
In the reverse order (*vyutkrama*), the euphonic junction (*saṃdhi*) is like that in the forward order; it is held to begin with *kṣaipra* and so on.
That is the prescription for the letter *ḍa* and so forth, which is the transformation ending in its vowel. 10.
In the reverse order of the sandhi of words, there is no *pragṛhya* status for those ending in the three vowels (*e*, *ai*, *o*), for *pragṛhya* vowels, or for vocatives ending in *u*. However,
an *a* followed by *e* or *o* undergoes *abhinihita* sandhi.
In cases of transposition and likewise in regular order, there are nine instances of the omission of *kampa*.

In the case of a reversed *saṃdhi*, in a *praśliṣṭa* [saṃdhi], and in *kṣaipra* and *abhinihita* [saṃdhis], one should exclude the *jātya* accent; thus, the prohibition of *kampa* applies to these three.

In this context, the prescription of the acute (udātta) and other accents for the *parigraha* and *avagraha* sections, as well as for words beginning with double-accented (*dvyudātta*) terms, is that which was stated by Śaunaka.
Furthermore, in the eighth syllable of the pāda "ādityair yātam," there shall be [an acute accent].
In the *padapāṭha*, that which is unaccented (*anudātta*) becomes as if accented (*udāttavat*) in the *saṃhitā*.
Having recited two words in sequence, then out of order, and then again in sequence, joined with the characteristics of accentuation as in the *saṃhitā*, that is called *jaṭā*. 15–16.
Thus ends the *Jaṭāpaṭalakārikā*.
